Carriers and shippers usually seek to optimize their profits/efficiency/
customer service. It is likely, even with more competitors under an expanded
C/Z-T/A system, that shipment movements would be planned in a manner designed
to provide efficient high quality service. But there would likely be certain inefficiencies and idle equipment as change occurs and the carrier system adjusts to new
standards. It is not improbable to expect certain elements of "destructive competition"
to develop and for some carriers to find considerable difficulty in coping with such an\nenvironment on traditional terms and to be faced with the prospect of either making
substantial readjustments or of leaving the marketplace.
A major difference between the intercity and local transportation scenes is in the lack of alternatives to costly interlining at the local level and in the greater fluctuation in the origins/destinations/quantities/numbers/variety of shipments at the local level. Consequently, flexibility to respond and adapt to a greater variety of situations is felt to be a need at the local level. The estimates by short-haul carriers of how much traffic they may lose as a result of larger C/Z's-T/A's are in some respects—to the extent the losses would result from elimination of interlining—indicative of the efficiencies that could be achieved with larger C/Z's-T/A's.
Adoption of the proposed population-mileage formula should result in both

(a) the substantial reduction in interlining predicted by the firms/associations/\ninstitutions whose representations were in favor of the expanded population-mileage
formula, and (b) the greater flexibility of carriers to adapt and respond.
Should the decision be in favor of an expanded population-mileage formula, the economic impacts could be softened and extended through implementation of the increased mileages on a graduated basis.
